evidence_set: Cutaneous vascular conductance is the laser-Doppler forearm blood-flow signal divided by mean arterial pressure, normalized to the maximum at that site; it is not flow alone. Site maximum was assessed after local skin heating to 42°C for 30 minutes. Results text at the stated highest common oesophageal temperature, 37.86°C, gives conductance 49±9 versus 70±5% of maximum (P=.03), and sweat rate 0.8±0.2 versus 1.0±0.1 mg/cm²/min (P=.04), for cocaine versus lidocaine. Seven people were enrolled, but the number contributing to this highest-temperature comparison is not stated. Independent approximate readings of the final curves on a 300dpi Figure 2 are about 54–55 versus 67% of maximum and about 0.86 versus 1.05 mg/cm²/min; these plotted endpoints differ numerically from the text values. The Figure 2 legend states mean±SE and P<.01 for cocaine versus lidocaine. Statistical Analysis describes two-way repeated-measures analysis of responses throughout heat stress, but the legend does not specify whether its P label denotes that full-response comparison or a particular temperature/endpoint comparison. The different significance labels therefore do not prove inconsistent results for the same endpoint test. The reported information does not resolve the numerical text/plot discrepancy, and no reconciled analysis is substituted. Figure 1’s mean lidocaine curve also ends below 37.86°C.

Measurements, forearm laser-Doppler measurement and cutaneous vascular conductance definition (printed p.786, PDF p.2); Experimental Protocol, site maximum and normalization, and Statistical Analysis (printed p.787, PDF p.3); Results third paragraph and Figure 1 bottom panel and legend (printed p.788, PDF p.4); Figure 2 and legend (printed p.789, PDF p.5).
